analysis.one_liner: Taxes stock, bond, and derivatives trades at 0.005% to 0.5%, with the tax refunded to households earning under $50,000.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Ways and Means Committee: no hearing, no vote, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The Inclusive Prosperity Act would put a small tax on every trade of stocks (0.5% of the value), bonds (0.1%), and derivatives (0.005%). The money raised would go to the Treasury, and the bill states the revenue would be available for the social safety net, infrastructure, Medicare and Medicaid, education, housing aid, and clean energy. Anyone whose income is under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples) would get a tax credit refunding the trading tax they paid, so the bill aims the cost at large and frequent traders rather than small investors. It also exempts new stock and bond offerings and short-term debt so it does not tax companies raising capital.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income households, who would be reimbursed for any trading tax they paid through a credit for anyone earning under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples) [S2][S3]. Public programs would gain a new funding stream: the bill's stated purposes include strengthening the safety net, child care, Social Security, expanded Medicare and Medicaid, education and student debt relief, housing assistance, infrastructure, and clean energy [S3]. Pension and retirement savers benefit from the stated goal of curbing short-term speculation that the bill's findings link to financial instability [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The tax is levied on each transfer of ownership in stocks, partnership interests, bonds, and derivatives: 0.5% on stocks and partnership interests, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives, paid by the exchange, clearinghouse, or broker rather than the individual investor [S3].
Individuals with modified adjusted gross income of $50,000 or less ($75,000 on a joint return) get a credit for the full amount of trading tax they paid, so small investors are made whole [S2][S3].

The bill states the revenue would be available for the social safety net, child care, Social Security, expanded Medicare and Medicaid, education, student debt relief, housing assistance for low-income households, infrastructure, transit, and clean energy [S3].
New stock and bond issues are exempt, and debt with a maturity of 60 days or less is excluded, so companies raising capital and routine short-term money markets are not taxed [S3].
The bill's findings cite the precedent of a U.S. stock transfer tax that existed from 1914 to 1966 and note that about 40 countries levy a financial transactions tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Frequent traders and financial firms bear the cost. The tax is collected by trading venues and brokers on every covered transaction [S3]. Large banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms that trade constantly would pay the most, and part of the cost would be passed to investors in the form of slightly wider trading spreads and fund costs; investors earning above $50,000 would not get the credit. In theory, some trading could move to overseas venues to avoid the tax, shrinking the revenue base.
analysis.who_pays_short: Frequent traders and big financial firms

drawbacks.text: The bill does not appropriate the revenue to any specific program; it only states the money 'will be available to' a list of purposes, so Congress could later spend it on anything, and the bill itself raises no program dollar [S3].

A tax on every trade raises costs for all investors, including retirement accounts and mutual funds whose managers trade regularly; only households earning $50,000 or less get the credit back, so savers above that line absorb the cost in fund expenses and spreads [S3].

Derivatives are taxed at only 0.005% and short-term debt is exempt, so a large share of trading volume in the fastest-moving markets escapes most of the tax, and critics of such taxes argue trading and revenue both shrink as activity shifts abroad.

The bill's own findings claim the tax could raise 'hundreds of billions annually,' an estimate that assumes trading volumes stay near current levels; independent estimates of financial transaction taxes generally project smaller amounts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is a broad, small tax on the most profitable trading activity, with the smallest investors explicitly protected by a refund credit and new capital raises exempted. The main honest concerns are that the revenue figures in the findings are optimistic, that costs leak to mid-income savers through fund and trading costs, and that the bill never specifies how the money would actually be spent. As written it is a funding-eligibility bill, not a spending bill, so its benefits depend entirely on future Congresses choosing to use the revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on September 14, 2012, less than two months before the end of the congressional session, with six original cosponsors [S3][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on September 14, 2012, and that is the last action in its record: no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].
It drew 16 cosponsors, all Democrats, in a House where Republicans held the majority and controlled the committee calendar [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Frequent traders, investment banks, hedge funds, and derivatives dealers kept trading free of any transaction tax, and no new revenue stream for safety-net or infrastructure spending was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big financial firms kept trading tax-free

industries.industry: Investment banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms
industries.note: These firms execute the most trades and would pay the bulk of the tax on every stock purchase (0.5%) and bond purchase (0.1%). The bill's findings argue the tax would also curb the short-term speculation they profit from [S3].

Derivatives, currency, and index contracts are taxed at 0.005% per transaction, with payments treated as separate taxable transactions. The rate is far lower than on stocks but reaches the largest notional market.

Exchanges and clearinghouses would be responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on trades that occur on their facilities, adding compliance work without themselves bearing the tax, except on their own transactions.
Brokers must pay the tax on customer trades executed off-exchange and handle reporting. Some cost would pass to customers, but households earning under $50,000 would be refunded through the credit.
Fund managers trade continuously, and the tax would add costs passed to shareholders. The credit only protects households earning $50,000 or less, so savers above that threshold absorb the cost.
